connections.observation: παρανομία first slips in disguised as play (ἐν παιδιᾶς γε μέρει), making play itself appear harmless (s002). The counter-requirement is that children receive more lawful play (ἐννομωτέρου παιδιᾶς) from the start (s003). The same word—παιδιά—holds both the disguise and the remedy.

παρανομία enters small (κατὰ σμικρόν) and steps out larger (μείζων ἐκβαίνει) through the six-verb sequence (s004). The small/large contrast recurs (s012): small customs (τὰ σμικρά) are rediscovered by the well-educated, diseases grow greater (μείζω) under futile treatment, and the greatest legislation (μέγιστα) is reserved for Apollo. The progression from small entry to large overthrow is answered by small customs genuinely preserved and greatest matters rightly deferred.

συμβόλαια appears first as the stage where lawlessness emerges from private habits (s005, 424d). εὐνομία corrects (ἐπανορθοῦσα) what was previously neglected in the city (s007, 425a). Later, futile legislators endlessly correct (ἐπανορθούμενοι, ἐπανορθοῦντες) the very συμβόλαια where lawlessness had emerged (s005, 425c–426e; s007). The same verb—ἐπανορθόω—names genuine correction once and futile patching twice, both touching the same site: συμβόλαια.

Socrates refuses to legislate (νομοθετεῖν) small customs (s006, 425b), declines again for marketplace contracts (425c, 425d), and finally reserves the greatest, finest, and first legislation (μέγιστα καὶ κάλλιστα καὶ πρῶτα τῶν νομοθετημάτων) for Apollo (s006, 427b). The refusals bracket the small; the deferral names the great (s012).

The sick who refuse to leave their bad regimen are called χαριέντως engaged (s009, 426a) while doctoring accomplishes nothing and diseases grow (s008). Their hatred of truth-telling is declared not χαρίεν (s009, 426a, 426b). Cities that flatter such behavior χαρίζηται to citizens (s009, 426c). Futile legislators are called most χαριέστατοι (s009, 426e) while cutting the Hydra of wrongdoing in contracts (s008 implied through context). χαρίεις shifts from ironic charm to denied grace to flattery to superlative irony across the medical cluster.

θεραπεία first names care of parents among small customs (s010, 425b), then flattering service to badly governed cities (s010, 426c), then ritual service to gods, daimones, and heroes (θεραπεῖαι, s010, 427b; s014). The final θεραπεῖαι belong to Apollo (s013), the πάτριος ἐξηγητής. The word moves from domestic custom through political flattery to divine cult, all three contexts preserved.

The φυλακτήριον to be built (οἰκοδομητέον) for the guardians in music (s001, 424d) uses architectural language. Apollo sits (καθήμενος) at the earth's navel (ὀμφαλοῦ) as πάτριος ἐξηγητής (s013, 427c). The built fortress in music and the seated god at the world's center are the section's two spatial fixtures—one a task, one a given.

Futile legislators cut the Hydra (Ὕδραν τέμνουσιν, s011, 426e) while endlessly correcting (ἐπανορθοῦντες, s007, 426e). The mythical image and the repeated verb name the same futility: cutting produces more heads; correcting produces more need for correction.

The dense list of small customs—silence, reclining, rising, parental care, haircuts, cloaks, shoes, bodily bearing (s015, 425b)—is immediately followed by the claim that legislating them is foolish (νομοθετεῖν δʼ αὐτὰ οἶμαι εὔηθες, s006, 425b). The list's length and specificity make visible what will not be legislated.

Like calls to like (τὸ ὅμοιον ὂν ὅμοιον παρακαλεῖ, s016, 425c). Children who play well (καλῶς ἀρξάμενοι παῖδες παίζειν, s003, 425a) receive εὐνομία through music, and everything that follows is like in kind. The principle of sameness producing sameness grounds the claim that rightly begun play yields lawful consequences.

τελευτάω appears as lawlessness finally overturning everything (τελευτῶσα, s017, 424e), as education issuing finally in something complete (τελευτῶν … τέλεον, s017, 425c), and as the dead requiring burial (τελευτησάντων … θῆκαι, s017, s014, 427b). The verb shifts from metaphorical culmination to literal death; the dead's θῆκαι belong among Apollo's νομοθετήματα (s014).

Those who will not stop drinking, gorging, sex, and idleness (μεθύων καὶ ἐμπιμπλάμενος καὶ ἀφροδισιάζων καὶ ἀργῶν, s018, 426a) consider the truth-teller most hateful. No drugs, cautery, surgery, incantations, or amulets will help (s008, 426b). The fourfold list of intemperate acts is met by a fivefold list of useless remedies; truth-telling is the refused remedy not listed among the medical ones.

παρανομία's infiltration sequence (s004) ends with τελευτῶσα overturning everything (s017, 424e). εὐνομία's counter-sequence ends with τελευτῶν issuing in something τέλεον—complete or fulfilled (s017, 425c). Both progressive movements culminate, but one overturns (ἀνατρέψῃ) and the other completes (τέλεον). τελευτάω names both outcomes.

The greatest, finest, and first legislation (τά γε μέγιστα καὶ κάλλιστα καὶ πρῶτα τῶν νομοθετημάτων, s006, s013, 427b) belongs to Apollo. Socrates and the interlocutors do not know (οὔτʼ ἐπιστάμεθα) these things when founding a city and will use no other interpreter (ἐξηγητῇ) than the ancestral one (τῷ πατρίῳ, s013, 427c). πάτριος appears twice; ἐξηγητής and ἐξηγεῖται frame the god's role. The deferral is grounded in acknowledged ignorance and ancestral custom, not merely in the matters' importance.

elements.context: οὐδὲ χρησόμεθα ἐξηγητῇ ἀλλʼ ἢ τῷ πατρίῳ
πάτριος ἐξηγητὴς ἐν μέσῳ τῆς γῆς

new_signals.observation: ἐξηγητής recurs twice and its verb ἐξηγέομαι once in rapid succession, naming Apollo's interpretive role at Delphi.

elements.context: ἐννόμους τε καὶ σπουδαίους … ἄνδρας αὐξάνεσθαι ἀδύνατον ὄν
ἐν τῇ μὲν ὅτι ἀνωφελῆ καὶ πλέον οὐδέν

new_signals.observation: ἀδύνατον and ἀνωφελῆ both name impossibility or uselessness: lawful men cannot grow from lawless play; legislating small matters in a badly governed city is profitless.
λανθάνει names how lawlessness slips in unnoticed; ἐξηπάτηνται names those deceived by the many's praise into thinking themselves political. Both verbs mark forms of undetected error.
